paras: The lynching of Phil Davis, Walter Carter and Clint Thomas was the hanging of three Black men near Belcher, Caddo Parish, Louisiana, on November 30, 1903, before a crowd reported at about 1,200 people. The men were accused of taking part in the shooting of Robert Adger, a white planter and merchant who died a week later. Papers across the country noted that Black residents had joined the hunt and that whites gave one of them a $100 purse, a detail the Black press condemned.

According to the Bossier Banner, Robert E. Adger was about 46, a planter and merchant, and the son of one of Bossier Parish's most eminent citizens. Wire reports called him "one of the most popular business men in North Louisiana" and placed Belcher twenty miles from Shreveport.

Adger was shot at Belcher on the night of November 28; the first report said the shooters were "two unknown persons who escaped." A Shreveport dispatch the next day said five Black men were implicated, that three had been caught within ten miles while posses pursued two toward De Soto Parish, and that citizens had hidden the captives "to prevent the authorities from rescuing them."

According to the Associated Press, Davis and Carter were captured several miles from the scene and Thomas about a mile and a half from Belcher. Brought before the wounded Adger, the men were said to have confessed that they had been "trying new guns" and turned them on him in the street. About 1 p.m. on November 30 they were taken from concealment and hanged from a single limb of a tree, without shots fired, after being allowed to pray. Two other men under arrest, Sam Lee and Peter Thomas, were released. The wire added that Black residents of Belcher joined the search and that one received a $100 purse from whites for his part in the pursuit.
Adger died of his wounds on December 7 and was buried at Cottage Grove cemetery. No report of an inquest, arrests of the lynchers or a grand jury inquiry appears in the coverage.

The first dispatch ran on November 30 under headlines such as "Lynching Rumored in Louisiana Town" in the Birmingham Age-Herald and "Mob Hides Negro Suspects" in the Beatrice Daily Express. The Associated Press account of the hanging appeared on December 1 from Washington and Savannah to Salt Lake City and Honolulu. The Savannah Morning News headlined "Three Strung Up" over "Negroes Had Confessed the Fatal and Unprovoked Shooting," and the Wyoming Tribune said the three "Pay Penalty for Their Crime." Weekly digests carried one-line versions into late December, several placing Belcher in Mississippi.

Southern comment accepted the confession: the Southern Sentinel of Winnfield, Louisiana, wrote that the men "were promptly dealt with," and the Gainesville Star described "bad negroes" whose neighbors joined the whites in the lynching. A few reprint headlines struck another note, as when the Manning Times called it "a Triple Lawless Execution."

In the Black press, the Cleveland Gazette printed only the one-line Shreveport item. The Colored American called the purse "blood money" and the lynchers "human tigers." The Richmond Planet named the three men, said the hanging "partook of the nature of a picnic," and told Black participants they had condoned "nothing more nor less than murder," closing "Lynch-law must go!" A week later the Planet answered a Washington Post editorial alarmed at Black participation in the lynching.

Accounts of the shooting differ: the Shreveport follow-up said Adger was quelling a street disturbance, The Sun's New Orleans dispatch said he was stopping a fight among cotton pickers on his plantation, and the AP version, drawn from the confession, said the men were trying new guns. The Sun also said the mob took the three from a posse trying to reach the parish jail and that two others escaped to Shreveport. Most reports dated the lynching Monday, November 30, though The Sun implied November 29 and one digest said Sunday. Wire copies spoke of a "fatal shooting" and the Southern Sentinel of an "attempt on the life"; the Bossier Banner's obituary shows Adger was alive at the lynching.

reader.title: Lynching of Phil Davis, Walter Carter and Clint Thomas
bases: Three Black men accused of shooting a white planter were taken from or kept away from the authorities and hanged from a tree before a crowd of about 1,200 (A16, A18, A13).

Phil Davis, Walter Carter and Clint Thomas were hanged without trial by a crowd of about 1,200 after citizens hid them from the authorities (A3, A16), and the papers said they were 'executed' for their part in shooting Robert Adger, a punitive pretext (A16, A18, A28).

The Associated Press report (A16, A18), an independent New Orleans dispatch in The Sun (A13), the Louisiana Southern Sentinel (A28) and the Black press (A34) agree that three Black men were lynched at Belcher over the shooting of Adger, though they differ on details.

accounts.label: First Shreveport report
accounts.gist: Adger was shot and mortally wounded by two unknown persons who escaped.

accounts.label: Shreveport wire, Nov 29
accounts.gist: Five Black men implicated; Adger shot six times quelling a street disturbance; three caught and hidden by citizens from the authorities with lynching openly intended; two pursued toward De Soto Parish.

accounts.label: Associated Press, Nov 30
accounts.gist: Davis, Carter and Thomas confessed to firing new guns at Adger, were hidden until about 1 p.m. and hanged from one limb before 1,200 whites and Black people; Lee and Peter Thomas released; a Black man rewarded with $100.

accounts.label: New Orleans dispatch (The Sun)
accounts.gist: Adger was shot by five cotton pickers while stopping a fight on his plantation; two escaped to Shreveport; three captured at Dixie were taken by the mob from a posse trying to get them to the parish jail.

accounts.label: Louisiana weekly
accounts.gist: The three were hanged Monday for an attempt on Adger's life Saturday night after confessing when confronted by him.

accounts.label: Black editorial comment
accounts.gist: The Colored American and Richmond Planet took the wire's facts as given and condemned the lynching, the $100 reward and the part played by Black residents.

framing.detail: Savannah Morning News: 'Three Strung Up' over 'Negroes Had Confessed the Fatal and Unprovoked Shooting of Robert Adger'.
Wyoming Tribune headline: 'Three Lynched Negroes Who Practiced With Rifles on White Man Pay Penalty for Their Crime'.
Southern Sentinel said the men 'were promptly dealt with'; the Gainesville Star wrote of 'bad negroes' and Black participation.
Times-Dispatch 'Three Swing to One Limb', with 'Twelve Thousand' in the headline; many papers ran the AP text unchanged.
The Sun's New Orleans dispatch noted the effort to take the men to jail and that the mob would not allow it.
Some reprint headlines were critical: Manning Times 'a Triple Lawless Execution'; Lincoln County Record 'Louisiana Mob Advancing in the "Art of Lynching."'
Cleveland Gazette ran a one-line Shreveport item in its news column.
Colored American called the $100 purse 'blood money' and the lynchers 'human tigers'.
Richmond Planet: the hanging 'partook of the nature of a picnic', Black participants condoned 'murder', 'Lynch-law must go!'

conflicts.note: The AP report filed the same afternoon from Shreveport is the most direct; the Tuesday variant is a reprint in a weekly a week later.
